entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: Even if [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] even if [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the even if clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Grants a condition the maximum benefit of the doubt and says the main clause holds anyway. The distinction learners need is with even though: Even though it rained, we went means it rained, while Even if it rains, we're going leaves the rain an open possibility.
examples: Even if the flight leaves on time, we'll miss the connection in Denver.
She would have taken the job even if they had offered less.
Even if you apologize now, the damage is done.
I'm walking there even if it's ten degrees out.
Even if every member votes yes, the measure still needs the governor's signature.
He wouldn't sell the house even if somebody offered him double.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.register: neutral, though editors usually change it to unless
entries.clause: adverbial clause of negative condition (exception)
entries.pattern: [main clause] except if [clause]. · Except if [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] except when [clause]. · [main clause] except where [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it when it follows the main clause, which is where it nearly always sits; comma after it on the rare occasions the clause is fronted.
entries.meaning: Carves an exception out of a statement that otherwise holds — the same job unless does in one word instead of two. American editors treat it as wordy and swap in unless, and it earns its keep in only two places: where the exception is one of several being listed in parallel (except if, except when, except where), and where unless would be read as conditioning the whole sentence rather than the one item it is attached to.
examples: The office is open every weekday except if it's a federal holiday.
Don't call me at work except if it's an emergency.
Coverage continues except if the premium goes unpaid for sixty days.
Returns are accepted within thirty days except if the tag has been removed.
She answers every email the same day, except if she's traveling.
Except if the weather turns, the crew works straight through Saturday.

entries.type: subordinating (also a complementizer in indirect questions)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition; also a noun clause (indirect yes/no question)
entries.pattern: If [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] if [clause]. · [verb of knowing or asking] if [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted if clause; normally no comma when the if clause follows. Never put a comma before if introducing a noun clause: I don't know if he's coming.
entries.meaning: The all-purpose conditional. The word itself never changes to show how likely the condition is — the tense of its clause does that job, with the present for real conditions, the simple past for unlikely ones, and the past perfect for impossible ones. Note that a future condition takes the present tense: If it rains tomorrow, never If it will rain tomorrow.
examples: If it rains tomorrow, the game moves to Sunday.
Call me if you get lost.
If I had left ten minutes earlier, I would have made the train.
She'd take the promotion if they moved her back to Denver.
If you're finished with that, I'll take it.
Let me know if the package arrives.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition (biconditional)
entries.pattern: [main clause] if and only if [clause]. · [proposition] iff [proposition] (written mathematics and logic only).
entries.punctuation: No commas at all — the phrase is doing precise work and a comma weakens the link. It sits after the main clause; fronting it is not idiomatic.
entries.meaning: States that the condition is both sufficient and necessary, closing both directions at once. Plain if gives only sufficiency and only if only necessity, so this is the one that says the two statements stand or fall together.
examples: A triangle is equilateral if and only if all three of its angles are equal.
An integer is even if and only if its last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.
The grant is renewed if and only if the recipient files an annual report.
Payment becomes due if and only if the goods arrive undamaged.
A set is closed iff it contains all of its limit points.
The clause is triggered if and only if both parties sign before the deadline.

entries.type: subordinating (elliptical — unless with the negated main clause left unsaid)
entries.register: neutral; the standalone reply is conversational
entries.clause: an unless clause with its negative main clause reduced to the bare not
entries.pattern: Not unless [clause]. (a complete turn in conversation) · [negative main clause], not unless [clause]. · [negative main clause] — not unless [clause].
entries.punctuation: As a standalone reply it takes a period and no internal comma. Tacked onto a negative statement it reads as an afterthought and takes a comma or a dash in front of it. It never takes a comma inside the pair.
entries.meaning: Answers a question by naming the one condition that would turn the no into a yes — unless with the refusal left implicit. It is the conversational twin of only if: Not unless she asks and Only if she asks set the same terms, one as a refusal and one as a policy.
examples: "Are you going to the reunion?" "Not unless Danny goes."
"Can we still get a table?" "Not unless somebody cancels."
He isn't signing anything, not unless his lawyer reads it first.
The plant doesn't reopen — not unless the inspection clears.
"Will she change her mind?" "Not unless you apologize first."
We're not driving up there in February, not unless the roads are clear.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition (necessary condition)
entries.pattern: [main clause] only if [clause]. · Only if [clause] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma before only if when it follows the main clause. When it is fronted it triggers subject–auxiliary inversion in the main clause and takes no comma: Only if you ask will she tell you.
entries.meaning: Marks the condition as necessary rather than merely sufficient — nothing else will do. If you sign, we ship leaves other routes open; We ship only if you sign closes them all.
examples: We'll refund the deposit only if you cancel a week in advance.
Only if the tests come back clean will they reopen the plant.
He answers his phone only if he recognizes the number.
The policy pays out only if the damage exceeds the deductible.
Only if both parents sign can the child travel alone.
You may retake the exam only if you attend the review session.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of negative condition (exception)
entries.pattern: [main clause] unless [clause]. · Unless [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted unless clause; normally no comma when it follows. The clause takes the present tense for future conditions, never will.
entries.meaning: Means "except on the condition that" — it carves one exception out of a statement that otherwise holds. It is close to if … not but narrower: unless names the single circumstance that would overturn the main clause, and it cannot be used for counterfactuals (If I hadn't called…, never Unless I had called…).
examples: The store closes at six unless there's a holiday sale.
Unless somebody objects, I'll book the room for Thursday.
Don't sign anything unless your lawyer has read it.
We'll be there by noon unless traffic on the interstate is terrible.
Unless you've already eaten, there's a plate in the oven.
She never takes a day off unless she's genuinely sick.

entries.type: subordinating (fixed doublet)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time and condition at once
entries.pattern: [main clause] as and when [clause]. · [main clause] as and when [past participle or adjective]. · As and when [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it when it follows the main clause, which is where it almost always sits; comma after a fronted clause. Never split the three words with a comma — they work as one conjunction.
entries.meaning: A drafter's doublet meaning "at whatever times, and each time that" — it leaves the schedule of an obligation open instead of fixing a date, and it covers repetition as well as timing. Against if and when, which doubts the event will happen at all, as and when takes it for granted and questions only the calendar: payable as and when the invoices fall due assumes there will be invoices.
examples: Dividends are payable as and when declared by the board.
The contractor will submit invoices as and when the work is completed.
Rent shall be paid as and when it falls due.
Additional units will be released as and when demand warrants.
The trustee may sell the securities as and when she thinks fit.
As and when further records come to light, the docket will be updated.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition (also of time — see below)
entries.pattern: [main clause] as long as [clause]. · As long as [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted as long as clause; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Sets a standing requirement: the main clause holds for exactly as many cases as the condition does. The same three words also measure duration (Stay as long as you like), and only the sense of the sentence tells them apart — the conditional reading describes a state of affairs, the temporal one describes a stretch of time.
examples: You can borrow the truck as long as you bring it back with a full tank.
As long as everyone's comfortable with the date, I'll send the invitations.
The warranty holds as long as you keep the receipt.
So long as the numbers hold up, we'll expand in the fall.
I don't care where we eat as long as it isn't that pizza place again.
He'll keep quiet about it as long as nobody asks him directly.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase, a gerund, or a whether clause)
entries.clause: no clause of its own — a noun phrase, an -ing phrase, or a whether clause naming what the outcome hangs on
entries.pattern: [main clause] contingent on [noun phrase]. · [main clause] contingent on [gerund]. · [main clause] contingent on whether [clause]. · Contingent on [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it when it follows the main clause, which is where it almost always sits. Comma after the phrase when it is fronted. Never put a comma between contingent and on.
entries.meaning: Hangs an outcome on something else happening, named as a noun rather than spelled out as a clause. It is the close cousin of subject to, and contracts use the two almost interchangeably, but they point at different things: subject to defers to a rule or an approval that already exists, while contingent on waits on a future event that may never occur. Note that contingent is an adjective outside this use, and a noun in a contingent of volunteers.
examples: The offer is contingent on the buyer securing financing.
Her bonus is contingent upon hitting the third-quarter target.
Contingent on board approval, we'll announce the merger Monday.
Everything is contingent on whether the permit comes through.
The second payment is contingent on delivery of a working prototype.
Federal funding is contingent on the state's matching the grant dollar for dollar.

entries.type: subordinating (fixed doublet)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition and time at once
entries.pattern: [main clause] if and when [clause]. · If and when [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted if and when clause; no comma when it follows. Never split the pair with a comma — the three words work as one conjunction. Like plain if, the clause takes the present tense for future conditions, never will.
entries.meaning: The positive mirror of unless and until: it leaves the whether and the when open at once and promises nothing about either. That doubt is the whole difference from plain when — We'll deal with it when he calls expects the call, if and when he calls does not.
examples: We'll cross that bridge if and when we come to it.
If and when the funding clears, we'll start hiring.
The company will comment if and when the investigation ends.
If and when she decides to sell, she has my number.
Those shares vest if and when the merger closes.
I'll worry about the tax bill if and when it actually shows up.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition
entries.pattern: [main clause] on condition that [clause]. · On condition that [clause], [main clause] (rare).
entries.punctuation: No comma before it when it follows the main clause, which is where it almost always sits. On the rare occasions the clause is fronted, a comma follows it. Formal writing often puts the base-form subjunctive in the clause: on condition that he stay, not stays.
entries.meaning: States a term that somebody imposes — a stipulation attached to a permission or a deal, so there is always a grantor standing behind it. Provided that merely names a requirement; on condition that implies that a person set it.
examples: He agreed to testify on condition that his name never appear in print.
The museum accepted the collection on condition that it be displayed together.
She'll release the recording on the condition that both parties approve the transcript.
They let him out on condition that he stay within the county.
The loan was granted on condition that the company cut its dividend.
On condition that the school keeps her name off the building, she'll fund the whole wing.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition (a shared expectation treated as a term)
entries.pattern: [main clause] on the understanding that [clause]. · [main clause] with the understanding that [clause]. · On the understanding that [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it when it follows the main clause, which is where it nearly always sits; comma after a fronted clause. A comma before it is possible when the qualification is an afterthought rather than part of the deal.
entries.meaning: Attaches a condition that both sides are taken to have agreed to without anyone writing it down — the softest member of the proviso family. On condition that names a term somebody imposed and can enforce; on the understanding that names an expectation, and the usual reason for saying it out loud is that the speaker suspects it may not be shared.
examples: She agreed to chair the committee on the understanding that it would meet twice a year.
We released the figures with the understanding that they would not be published before Monday.
The city leased the lot to the club on the understanding that the field stays open to the public.
He took the loan with the understanding that repayment would start after graduation.
On the understanding that nothing here is final, I'll circulate a draft this week.
They dropped the objection on the understanding that the hearing would be rescheduled, not canceled.

entries.type: subordinating (participial — frozen from the verb provide, which is why it never inflects here)
entries.register: neutral to formal (standard in rules and contracts)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition
entries.pattern: [main clause] provided (that) [clause]. · Provided (that) [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted provided (that) clause. When it follows, the comma is optional: use one if the proviso is an afterthought, none if it is part of the core statement. Legal drafting sets it off as ; provided, however, that… — a style worth avoiding everywhere else.
entries.meaning: Introduces a requirement that has to be met for the main clause to hold. It does the same job as if, but flags the condition as a stipulation rather than a possibility, which is why it prefers things somebody can actually control.
examples: You may return the item provided that you have the receipt.
Provided that nothing changes, the closing is on the ninth.
Employees can carry over vacation days provided they use them by March.
The city will fund the repairs providing that the county matches the grant.
Provided that both signatures are notarized, the transfer takes effect immediately.
She'll speak at the conference, provided her travel is covered.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase)
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase naming the condition
entries.pattern: [main clause] subject to [noun phrase]. · Subject to [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted subject to phrase; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Makes a statement conditional on an approval, a rule, or an event named as a noun. Because it takes a noun phrase, it cannot carry a subject and verb the way provided that can, which is exactly why contracts like it — the condition stays compact and quotable.
examples: The offer is subject to a satisfactory home inspection.
Subject to board approval, the merger closes in March.
All fares are subject to change without notice.
The permit was issued subject to three conditions.
Delivery dates are subject to availability.
Subject to the terms below, the license is worldwide and perpetual.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.register: neutral to formal (contracts, statutes, academic prose)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition limiting the scope of the main clause
entries.pattern: [main clause] to the extent that [clause]. · To the extent that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] only to the extent that [clause]. · [main clause] to the extent of [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it when it follows the main clause; comma after a fronted clause. Never put a comma inside the phrase, and do not write to the extent, that.
variants: if and to the extent that
entries.meaning: Makes the main clause true in proportion to how far the condition holds instead of all at once — it answers "how far?" rather than "whether?" That partial quality is the whole difference from if: The rule applies if it doesn't conflict with federal law is a yes-or-no test, while to the extent that it doesn't conflict keeps whatever part of the rule survives and drops the rest.
examples: State law governs to the extent that it does not conflict with the federal statute.
To the extent that the deposit covers the damage, no further payment is due.
The company will reimburse expenses to the extent that they are documented.
I agree with her to the extent that the schedule is unrealistic, but not about the budget.
To the extent that anyone remembers the case at all, they remember the dissent.
Coverage applies only to the extent that the loss exceeds the deductible.
related: if and to the extent that

entries.type: subordinating (fixed doublet)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition and time at once
entries.pattern: [main clause, usually negative] unless and until [clause]. · Unless and until [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted unless and until clause; no comma before it when it follows the main clause, which is where it usually sits. Never split the pair with a comma — the three words work as one conjunction.
entries.meaning: A lawyer's doublet that closes two gaps at once: nothing happens unless the condition is met, and nothing happens until it is met. Outside legal and administrative writing, plain until almost always says everything the sentence needs.
examples: No payment is due unless and until the work passes inspection.
The account stays frozen unless and until a court says otherwise.
Unless and until the tenant cures the default, the lease remains in breach.
The company will make no further comment unless and until the investigation concludes.
Benefits are suspended unless and until the claimant files the missing form.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional phrase plus complementizer)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition — a stipulation cutting back what was just granted
entries.pattern: [main clause], with the proviso that [clause]. · [main clause] with the proviso that [clause]. · [main clause] subject to the proviso that [clause]. · With the proviso that [clause], [main clause]. (rare)
entries.punctuation: A comma before it is usual, because the proviso is added to a grant already made; a comma after it is wrong, since what follows is its own clause. Comma after the phrase on the rare occasions it is fronted. Formal drafting uses the base-form subjunctive inside the clause: with the proviso that the work stop at seven, not stops.
entries.meaning: Names a limit attached to permission that has just been given, and announces in advance that the qualification is coming. Where provided that simply states a requirement, with the proviso that frames it as a carve-out from the grant, which is why it lives in minutes, resolutions, and letters of acceptance rather than in ordinary prose.
examples: The board approved the budget, with the proviso that the hiring freeze stay in place.
She accepted the appointment with the proviso that she could keep teaching one course.
The council granted the permit, with the proviso that work stop at seven each evening.
We'll fund the second year with the proviso that the first year's results are reviewed.
The library will take the collection, with the proviso that nothing be sold off.
He agreed to the interview with the proviso that the tape not be edited.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase)
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase naming what is missing
entries.pattern: Absent [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] absent [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted absent phrase, which is where it usually appears; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: An American legal-register preposition meaning "if there is no." It states a negative condition in two words, and it has spread from court opinions into policy writing and journalism, though it still sounds stiff in conversation.
examples: Absent a written agreement, the default rules apply.
The bill has no path forward absent bipartisan support.
Absent evidence of fraud, the court will not reopen the case.
Absent some change in the weather, the launch window closes tonight.
Enrollment will keep falling absent a serious recruiting effort.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase); frozen from the verb bar, so it never behaves like a live participle and takes no subject
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase naming the one thing that would prevent the outcome
entries.pattern: Barring [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] barring [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted barring phrase; a comma before it when it follows is optional and common.
entries.meaning: Means "unless there is" — it names the single event that would derail the main clause, which is why it attaches to confident predictions. It is the everyday cousin of absent, which sounds legal by comparison.
examples: Barring a last-minute delay, we land at six.
The roof should last another decade, barring a bad hailstorm.
Barring an injury, she'll start every game this season.
We're on schedule barring something we haven't thought of.
Barring a miracle, this bill dies in committee.

entries.type: subordinating (a frozen clause — need is a bare noun subject and be the old present subjunctive)
entries.register: neutral; common in speech and in ordinary writing
entries.clause: a fixed adverbial clause of condition that takes no subject, tense, or negation of its own
entries.pattern: [main clause] if need be. · If need be, [main clause]. · [main clause], if need be, [continuation].
entries.punctuation: Comma before it when it trails the main clause, since it reads as an afterthought; comma after it when it opens the sentence; commas on both sides in the middle of a clause. The phrase never inflects — there is no if need was and no if needs be in American English, the second being the British form.
entries.meaning: Marks a fallback the speaker is willing to resort to — "if it turns out to be necessary." It is a fossil: need is the subject noun and be the present subjunctive, which is why it cannot be put into any other tense. Against in case, which acts on a possibility ahead of time, if need be holds the action back and takes it only if the need actually shows up.
examples: I can drive you to the airport if need be.
If need be, we'll hold the meeting over Zoom.
The clinic will stay open past six, if need be, until everyone has been seen.
She'll testify if need be, though she'd rather not.
We can cut the last two slides if need be.
If need be, the county can draw on the emergency fund.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of precautionary condition
entries.pattern: [main clause] in case [clause]. · In case [clause], [main clause]. · in case of [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted in case clause; no comma when it follows. American English does not write in the case that for this sense.
entries.meaning: Marks a precaution taken in advance against a possibility, so the main clause happens first, because of that possibility. Compare if: Take an umbrella if it rains means wait and see, while Take an umbrella in case it rains means take it now.
examples: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
I wrote down the address in case my phone dies.
In case you're wondering, the meeting got moved to Thursday.
Leave a key with the neighbor just in case.
In case of fire, use the stairs.
She keeps a spare charger in her bag in case somebody needs one.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition
entries.pattern: In the event that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] in the event that [clause]. · in the event of [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: The formal-register equivalent of if, reserved for conditions that are occurrences rather than states — a cancellation, a default, a death, a claim. In ordinary prose it is longer than if without being any clearer.
examples: In the event that the flight is canceled, the airline will rebook you at no charge.
Benefits are paid to the beneficiary in the event of the policyholder's death.
In the event that neither candidate reaches a majority, the House chooses the president.
The deposit is refundable in the event that the inspection fails.
In the event of a power outage, the generator starts automatically.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of remote precautionary condition
entries.pattern: [main clause] on the off chance (that) [clause]. · On the off chance (that) [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it in ordinary use; a comma is fine when the phrase is tacked on as an afterthought. Comma after it when the whole clause is fronted.
entries.meaning: In case with the odds marked low — the speaker is hedging against something unlikely and admitting as much. That admission is the whole point of choosing this phrase over in case.
examples: I texted him on the off chance that he's still in town.
She applied on the off chance the position was still open.
We brought a cooler on the off chance that the power went out again.
I'm asking on the off chance you know somebody who does drywall.
He checks the numbers every Monday on the off chance he won.
On the off chance that she's already left, I'll try her cell instead.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase or a gerund)
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase or an -ing phrase naming the extreme measure that would change the outcome
entries.pattern: Short of [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] short of [noun phrase]. · Short of [gerund], [main clause]. · [main clause] short of [gerund].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted short of phrase, which is where it usually appears; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Names the extreme step that would be needed to change the outcome and implies that nothing less will do. It overlaps with barring, but the two run in opposite directions: barring a strike, the trains run on time names the one thing that could spoil a good outcome, while short of a strike, nothing gets management's attention names the one thing that could rescue a bad one. Outside this conditional use, short of is an ordinary adjective phrase meaning "not enough of" (short of cash, short of breath), and what follows tells the two apart: the conditional names an action or an event, the adjective names a supply.
examples: Short of a miracle, this bill dies in committee.
Short of selling the house, I don't see how they cover the bills.
There's nothing more I can do short of calling her myself.
Short of an act of Congress, that rule is not changing.
They tried everything short of replacing the engine.
Short of rewriting the whole chapter, I'm not sure how to fix it.

entries.type: subordinating (absolute construction — a subject plus a participle, with no conjunction present)
entries.register: neutral to formal (economics, science writing, argument)
entries.clause: an absolute phrase doing the work of an adverbial clause of condition
entries.pattern: All else being equal, [main clause]. · [main clause], all else being equal. · [subject], all else being equal, [verb phrase]. · Other things being equal, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens the sentence, which is where it usually sits; comma before it when it trails; commas on both sides in the middle. It is a phrase, not a conjunction, so it cannot join two independent clauses on its own — a comma splice here is the same error it is with otherwise.
entries.meaning: Freezes every factor except the one under discussion, so that a comparison can be made about that factor alone. It is the working-English form of ceteris paribus, and it hedges as much as it conditions: the speaker is conceding that in the world outside the sentence other things are rarely equal.
examples: All else being equal, the cheaper flight wins.
A heavier bat, all else being equal, produces a slower swing.
Other things being equal, students who read more write better.
All else being equal, I'd rather hire someone local.
Raising the price lowers demand, all else being equal.
All other things being equal, the shorter route should be faster — but it runs straight through downtown.

entries.type: subordinating (participial)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition (a premise taken for granted)
entries.pattern: Assuming (that) [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], assuming (that) [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. When it follows, a comma is usual, because the clause reads as a hedge added after the fact.
entries.meaning: Introduces a premise the speaker is provisionally treating as true in order to reason from it. Unlike if, it signals that the premise is unverified and worth flagging; unlike given that, it makes no claim that the premise is established.
examples: Assuming the numbers hold, we break even in the third quarter.
We'll be there by seven, assuming traffic isn't awful.
Assuming that she accepts, when would she start?
The plan works, assuming nobody quits between now and June.
Assuming no one objects, I'll go ahead and order the equipment.
He can finish by Friday, assuming that the parts arrive Monday.

entries.type: subordinating (participial — frozen from the past participle of give); also a preposition before a bare noun phrase
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition shading into cause
entries.pattern: Given (that) [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], given (that) [clause]. · given [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; a comma is usual when it follows, too, since it reads as a supplied premise.
entries.meaning: Sets out a premise as already established and reasons forward from it — halfway between if and because. Where assuming that flags the premise as unproven, given that presents it as agreed, which is why it drifts toward cause: Given that the road is closed, we'll take the long way is barely different from because.
examples: Given that the road is closed, we'll take the long way.
The turnout was impressive, given that it poured all morning.
Given the circumstances, I think she handled it well.
Given that nobody has objected in six weeks, I'll assume the plan is approved.
It's a fair price, given what the market has been doing.
Given that you've already paid, the balance is zero.

entries.type: subordinating (participial — frozen from the past participle of grant); bare granted is a conjunctive adverb
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: Granted (that) [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], granted that [clause]. · Granting that [clause], [main clause]. · Granted, [sentence].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. When the clause trails the main clause it takes a comma before it, because it reads as a concession added after the fact. Standing alone as a concession, Granted takes a comma after it and usually opens the sentence.
entries.meaning: Concedes a point for the sake of argument and then pushes past it: even accepting that the clause is true, the main clause still stands. Where given that accepts a premise and reasons from it, granted that accepts one and reasons against it.
examples: Granted that the design is elegant, it's still far too expensive to build.
Granted, the first season is slow, but it pays off.
Granting that the witness is credible, the timeline still doesn't work.
Granted that she had every reason to be angry, the email was a mistake.
He's the best closer we've had in years, granted that the bar was pretty low.
Granted that the numbers are only estimates, they all point the same direction.

entries.type: subordinating (fixed phrase heading a conditional proposal)
entries.clause: a conditional clause standing alone as a question
entries.pattern: How about if [clause]? · What about if [clause]? · How about [gerund]? · How about [noun phrase]?
entries.punctuation: Ends with a question mark even though nothing is inverted and no main clause follows. The fragment is standard in speech and in writing that reports speech, not an error.
entries.meaning: Floats a suggestion as a conditional question — "suppose we did this; would that work?" It differs from what if, which is as often a worry as a proposal (What if it rains?): how about if is nearly always an offer, and it expects an answer rather than a shudder.
examples: How about if we meet at six instead?
What about if I drive and you navigate?
How about if she takes the early shift this week?
"The nine o'clock is full." "How about if we fly out the night before?"
What about if we split it three ways?
How about if I call you back after the meeting?

entries.type: subordinating (from the imperative of the verb say)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition, usually with no that
entries.pattern: Say [clause] — [question or consequence]? · Say [clause]. [question]? · Let's say [clause]; [main clause]. · [phrase], say, [example].
entries.punctuation: The hypothetical clause is followed by a dash, a comma, or a period before the consequence. The separate "for example" say is fenced by commas on both sides: in a few days — say, Thursday.
entries.meaning: The conversational way to launch a hypothetical, meaning "suppose" and belonging to speech and casual writing where supposing that would sound stiff. It nearly always sets up a question or a thought experiment rather than a rule.
examples: Say you miss the connection — what's your backup?
Say we leave at five. Do we still hit rush hour?
Let's say the bid comes in over budget; then what?
Say somebody offered you the job tomorrow. Would you take it?
Give it a few days — say, until Thursday — and call them again.

entries.type: subordinating (participial)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of hypothetical condition
entries.pattern: Supposing (that) [clause], [main clause or question]? · Suppose [clause], [main clause or question]?
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause — often a dash or a question mark instead, since the construction usually sets up a question.
entries.meaning: Invites the listener to entertain a hypothetical, most often as the opening of a question. Unlike if, it is essentially clause-initial: We'd be stuck supposing the ferry stopped running does not work.
examples: Supposing the ferry stops running, how do we get back?
Suppose you had a week off — where would you go?
Supposing that the tests come back negative, what's the next step?
Suppose we split the difference and call it four hundred.
Supposing nobody shows up, do we still pay for the room?

entries.type: subordinating (fixed phrase heading a conditional fragment)
entries.clause: a conditional clause standing alone as a question
entries.pattern: What if [clause]? · What if [clause] — [consequence]? · [verb of asking] what if [clause].
entries.punctuation: Ends with a question mark even though there is no main clause and no inversion. The fragment is standard, not an error.
entries.meaning: Raises a hypothetical as a proposal or a worry, leaving the consequence for the listener to supply. Tense does the work: What if we leave early? proposes something real, while What if we left early? holds it further away.
examples: What if it rains on Saturday?
What if we just told them the truth?
What if the flight gets canceled — do we still have the hotel?
She kept asking what if nobody came.
So what if he's ten minutes late? The doors don't open until eight.
What if I said I could get you a table at seven?

entries.type: subordinating (participial — takes a noun phrase, or a full clause after whether, how, what, where, who)
entries.clause: no clause after the bare form — a noun phrase; a full clause after depending on whether and the other wh- words
entries.pattern: [main clause] depending on [noun phrase]. · [main clause], depending on [noun phrase]. · [main clause] depending on whether [clause]. · Depending on whether [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] depending on how / what / where / who [clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma before it is usual when the phrase is an afterthought qualifying the whole main clause (We'll leave Friday or Saturday, depending on the weather) and none when it is part of the core statement (The fee changes depending on the plan). Comma after a fronted clause.
entries.meaning: Says the outcome varies with the condition instead of simply switching on or off — the everyday American way to write according as. Against contingent on, which makes one outcome wait on one event, depending on keeps both branches live: Contingent on the vote, we expand means the expansion waits, while We expand or we don't, depending on the vote means either answer is a real answer.
examples: We'll drive or fly, depending on the weather.
The fee changes depending on whether you file jointly.
Depending on whether the grant comes through, the study runs one year or three.
She's either brilliant or impossible, depending on who you ask.
Delivery takes two to five days, depending on where you live.
The room seats forty or sixty, depending on how you set up the chairs.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional phrase plus complementizer)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: [main clause] regardless of whether [clause]. · Regardless of whether [clause], [main clause]. · regardless of [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it follows. Note that irregardless is nonstandard and should never appear in writing.
entries.meaning: Says the main clause holds on both branches of a yes/no split. Even if grants one branch and dismisses it; regardless of whether covers both explicitly, which is why contracts and policies prefer it.
examples: The fee is due regardless of whether you use the service.
Regardless of whether the funding comes through, the study goes forward.
She'd have said the same thing regardless of whether anyone was listening.
Regardless of the outcome, the audit findings stand.
Practice starts at six regardless of whether it's raining.

entries.type: complementizer; subordinating in the whether … or condition
entries.clause: noun clause (indirect yes/no question); adverbial clause of alternative condition
entries.pattern: [verb, noun, or adjective] whether [clause]. · [preposition] whether [clause]. · Whether [clause] [verb phrase] (the noun clause as subject). · Whether [clause] or [clause], [main clause]. · Whether [clause] or not, [main clause]. · whether to [infinitive].
entries.punctuation: No comma before a whether noun clause. When a whether … or pair opens the sentence as a condition, put a comma after it: Whether you like it or not, the rule stands.
entries.meaning: Frames a yes/no alternative rather than a single case. Against conditional if, it is the form that survives in four places if cannot go — after a preposition (depends on whether), before an infinitive (whether to go), as a subject (Whether he comes is up to him), and directly before or not. It also removes the ambiguity in Let me know if he calls, which can mean either "report either way" or "only in the event that he does."
examples: I can't tell whether she's joking.
It depends on whether the landlord approves the sublet.
Whether we drive or fly, we'll need to leave by noon.
She hasn't decided whether to accept the offer.
Whether he meant it or not, the comment landed badly.
Let me know whether the check cleared.
Whether the bond passes comes down to turnout in the suburbs.

entries.type: subordinating; also a complementizer in noun clauses
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition; also a noun clause
entries.pattern: Whether or not [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whether or not [clause]. · [verb, noun, or adjective] whether or not [clause] (the noun clause). · [main clause] whether [clause] or not (the split form).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it follows, and none before a noun clause.
entries.meaning: Locks in "in both cases": the outcome is the same on either branch. In the noun-clause use, or not is merely emphatic and can be dropped (I don't know whether (or not) he's coming); in the adverbial use it cannot, because dropping it changes the sentence.
examples: Whether or not you agree with the policy, you have to follow it.
The train leaves at six whether or not everyone is on board.
Whether or not it rains, the ceremony is outdoors.
I still don't know whether or not she got the message.
He's going to say something whether we ask him to or not.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase)
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase naming the decisive factor
entries.pattern: But for [noun phrase], [main clause with would or would have]. · [main clause] but for [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted but for phrase; no comma when it follows.
entries.meaning: Names the one factor without which the main clause would have gone the other way, so the main clause must carry would or would have. This but is not the coordinating conjunction — it is the older but meaning "except," and the construction is the "but-for test" of causation in American law.
examples: But for the storm, the ceremony would have been outdoors.
But for your help, I'd still be sitting in that parking lot.
The company would have folded in 2009 but for an emergency loan.
But for a clerical error, the deed would have been recorded in June.
She would never have applied but for a professor's encouragement.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase)
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase naming what made the difference
entries.pattern: If not for [noun phrase], [main clause with would]. · [main clause with would] if not for [noun phrase]. · If it weren't for [noun phrase], [main clause]. · If it hadn't been for [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, which is where it almost always sits; no comma when it trails the main clause.
entries.meaning: The everyday American counterfactual — plain English for but for. The longer clausal forms pin down the time: if it weren't for points at a present state, if it hadn't been for at a past event.
examples: If not for the traffic, we would have been on time.
If it weren't for the noise, this would be a perfect apartment.
If it hadn't been for her, nobody would have caught the mistake.
The season would have been a disaster if not for two late wins.
If it weren't for bad luck, he'd have no luck at all.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition; also an exclamative wish standing alone
entries.pattern: If only [clause with past or past perfect]! · If only [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], if only to [infinitive].
entries.punctuation: Period or exclamation point on the standalone wish; comma after the clause when a main clause follows. A comma before if only to when it trails the main clause.
entries.meaning: Expresses a wish that the condition were met, with the strong implication that it isn't — the verb shifts back one tense, so if only I had means I don't and if only I had had means I didn't. Unlike plain if, it needs no main clause: the regret is the whole sentence.
examples: If only I had known you were in town.
If only she'd asked, I would have driven her.
If only it were that simple.
If only the rent were two hundred dollars cheaper, I'd take the place.
Call him back, if only to end the argument.
If only we'd left an hour earlier.

entries.type: subordinating (inverted subjunctive with a prepositional complement)
entries.clause: no clause after for — a noun phrase; the condition is carried by the inverted were
entries.pattern: Were it not for [noun phrase], [main clause with would]. · [main clause with would] were it not for [noun phrase]. · Had it not been for [noun phrase], [main clause with would have].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, which is where it almost always sits; no comma when it trails the main clause. No if — the inversion replaces it, and writing if were it not for is an error.
entries.meaning: The formal, inverted counterfactual: the same content as if it weren't for, lifted in register by moving were in front of the subject. Were it not for takes a present or general state, had it not been for a past event.
examples: Were it not for the volunteers, the shelter would have closed years ago.
Had it not been for a delayed flight, they never would have met.
Were it not for her testimony, the case would have collapsed.
The town would be half its size were it not for the university.
Had it not been for the seatbelt, the injuries would have been far worse.

entries.type: subordinating (inverted past subjunctive plus a complementizer)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of counterfactual condition — a full clause, not a noun phrase
entries.pattern: Were it not that [clause], [main clause with would]. · [main clause with would] were it not that [clause]. · Had it not been that [clause], [main clause with would have].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause, which is where it almost always sits; no comma when it trails the main clause. No if — the inversion of were replaces it, and writing if were it not that is an error.
entries.meaning: The clause-taking twin of were it not for. Where were it not for names a thing (were it not for the rain), this one states a whole proposition (were it not that the rain had washed out the road), so it is the form to reach for when the decisive fact will not compress into a noun.
examples: Were it not that the roads were closed, we would have driven up that night.
The bill would have passed, were it not that two members were absent.
Were it not that she had kept every receipt, the audit would have gone badly.
I'd take the job tomorrow were it not that it means moving.
Had it not been that the alarm failed, the fire would have been caught in minutes.
The manuscript would be lost were it not that a copy went to the printer in March.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase or a gerund); also the ordinary preposition of lacking (coffee without sugar)
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase or an -ing phrase naming what is missing
entries.pattern: Without [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] without [noun phrase]. · Without [gerund], [main clause]. · [main clause] without [gerund].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted without phrase; no comma when it follows. No comma ever separates without from the noun phrase it governs.
entries.meaning: The plain-English member of the but for family, and the one word in it that nobody would call stiff. It names what is missing and lets the main clause say what follows. When the missing thing really is absent, the sentence is counterfactual and the main clause takes would (Without her, we'd have folded); when it is only hypothetical, the main clause stays in the present (Without a permit, you can't build). The conditional reading appears only when without governs the whole situation — in He left without saying goodbye it is the everyday preposition of lacking, modifying the verb, and no condition is being stated at all.
examples: Without the volunteers, the food bank would have closed in March.
You can't board without a valid ID.
Without a second income, they never would have kept the house.
The whole argument falls apart without that one footnote.
Without checking the tape, the referee would have missed the call.
She'd still be waiting on a diagnosis without her sister's pushing.

entries.type: subordinating by inversion — no conjunction present; the word is otherwise the auxiliary and main verb have
entries.register: neutral to formal in writing; uncommon in casual speech
entries.clause: adverbial clause of past counterfactual condition
entries.pattern: Had [subject] [past participle], [subject] would have [past participle]. · Had [subject] not [past participle], [main clause]. · [main clause with would have] had [subject] [past participle]. · uninverted: If [subject] had [past participle], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma between the inverted clause and the main clause when the inverted clause comes first, which is the usual order; no comma when it trails — We'd be there by now had we left ten minutes earlier. Never add if — write If I had known or Had I known, never both.
entries.meaning: Replaces if in past counterfactuals by moving the auxiliary had in front of the subject. The meaning is identical to if I had known, but the inverted form is more formal and more emphatic. Like the should and were inversions, it usually opens the sentence but can just as well follow the main clause. The negative cannot contract: Had I not known, never Hadn't I known, which is a question.
examples: Had I known you were coming, I would have made more food.
Had the company disclosed the defect, the recall would have been far smaller.
Had she not spoken up, the error would have gone into print.
Had we left ten minutes earlier, we'd be there by now.
Had the vote gone the other way, the whole department would have been reorganized.
I'd have driven you myself had I known your car was in the shop.

entries.type: subordinating by inversion — no conjunction present; the word is otherwise a modal auxiliary of obligation or expectation
entries.clause: adverbial clause of open future condition
entries.pattern: Should [subject] [bare infinitive], [main clause]. · [main clause] should [subject] [bare infinitive]. · uninverted: If [subject] should [bare infinitive], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma between the fronted inverted clause and the main clause; no comma when the inverted clause follows. Never combine the inversion with if.
entries.meaning: Marks a future condition as possible but not expected — the tentative conditional. It carries none of the obligation sense should has elsewhere: Should you need anything means "if you happen to need anything," not "you ought to need anything."
examples: Should you need anything, the front desk is open all night.
Should the shipment arrive damaged, photograph it before signing.
Should any of this change, I'll email everyone.
Should the tenant fail to pay, the landlord may terminate the lease.
Call this number should your symptoms return.

entries.type: subordinating by inversion — no conjunction present; the past subjunctive of be, which is otherwise just the plural and second-person past tense
entries.clause: adverbial clause of present or future counterfactual condition
entries.pattern: Were [subject] [complement], [main clause with would]. · Were [subject] to [infinitive], [main clause with would]. · [main clause with would] were [subject] [complement]. · uninverted: If [subject] were [complement], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma between the inverted clause and the main clause when the inverted clause comes first, which is the usual order; no comma when it trails — We'd start an hour later were it up to me. No if with the inversion, and no contraction: Were it not, never Weren't it.
entries.meaning: The past subjunctive were used for a hypothetical present or future, inverted in place of if. Were I you is the formal twin of if I were you, and were … to pushes the condition further into the unlikely future. The inverted clause normally comes first, but it can follow the main clause exactly as the had and should inversions do.
examples: Were I in your position, I'd ask for the raise in writing.
Were the bridge to close, the detour would add an hour.
Were she any less patient, that meeting would have ended in a fight.
Were it up to me, we'd start an hour later.
Were the company to relocate, most of the staff would not follow.
I'd say something to him myself were I not his sister.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (a pro-form standing in for a whether alternative)
entries.clause: no clause of its own — it points back at a two-branch condition already stated
entries.pattern: [sentence]. Either way, [sentence]. · [sentence]; either way, [sentence]. · [clause], but either way [clause]. · [main clause] either way (final, no comma).
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it, comma after it when it opens a clause — a comma alone in front of it is a comma splice, exactly as with otherwise and in that case. A coordinating conjunction may carry it instead, in which case the comma goes before the coordinator: You can pay now or at pickup, but either way the card has to match. Riding at the end of its own clause it takes no punctuation at all: The fee is the same either way.
entries.meaning: Answers a yes/no split already on the table by saying the outcome is the same on both branches — the pro-form counterpart of whether or not and regardless of whether, which spell the branches out instead of pointing back at them. It is strictly two-way: with three or more options open, in any case or regardless is the word.
examples: We can drive or fly; either way, we need to leave by noon.
He may take the offer or he may not. Either way, the position gets filled.
The fee is the same either way.
She might apologize, or she might dig in — either way, I'm done arguing about it.
You can pay now or at pickup, but either way the card has to match the ID.
Either way, somebody has to tell the landlord before Friday.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (participial phrase used as a connective)
entries.clause: no clause — it stands in for the whole condition just stated
entries.pattern: [sentence]. Failing that, [sentence]. · [sentence]; failing that, [sentence]. · [main clause] or, failing that, [alternative]. · Failing [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], failing which [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after failing that when it opens a sentence, and commas on both sides when it is parenthetical. It cannot join two independent clauses with a comma alone — use a period or a semicolon before it. Failing which is the exception in this entry: like in which case it heads a relative clause, so it takes an ordinary comma before it and no semicolon.
entries.meaning: Means "if that doesn't work": it points back at the option just named and introduces the fallback. It belongs to writing and planned speech — conversation uses if not or otherwise.
examples: Try the manager first; failing that, put your complaint in writing.
We'll fly out Thursday or, failing that, first thing Friday.
The parties will negotiate in good faith, failing which the dispute goes to arbitration.
Ask a librarian first and, failing that, try the county archive.
Failing a quorum, the vote is postponed to the next meeting.
Reset the router. Failing that, call the number on the back of the modem.

entries.type: subordinating (elliptical clause)
entries.clause: a reduced conditional clause — the verb is recovered from the previous sentence
entries.pattern: [statement or question]. If not, [main clause]. · [statement or question] — if not, [main clause]. · [statement]; if not, [main clause]. · [adjective or number], if not [stronger adjective or number].
entries.punctuation: Comma after If not when it opens a sentence, and a period, semicolon, or dash in front of it — a bare comma between the two clauses is a splice. In the scalar pattern the comma goes before if not and none after.
entries.meaning: Stands in for a whole negative condition already on the table: "if that is not the case." Keep it apart from the scalar if not, which raises the bar instead of negating — hundreds, if not thousands means possibly even thousands, not "otherwise thousands."
examples: Let me know by Friday. If not, I'll give the spot to somebody else.
Is the room free at two? If not, we can meet in the lobby.
Try the pharmacy on Third — if not, there's one by the hospital.
The repair will cost hundreds, if not thousands.
He's the best pitcher in the division, if not the league.

entries.type: subordinating (elliptical clause)
entries.clause: a reduced conditional clause standing in for a positive condition
entries.pattern: [statement or question]. If so, [main clause]. · [statement]; if so, [main clause]. · [main clause] if so.
entries.punctuation: Comma after If so when it opens a sentence. Like if not, it takes a period, a semicolon, or a dash in front of it, never a bare comma.
entries.meaning: Picks up a possibility just raised and says what follows from it, without repeating the clause. It is the compact written form of if that is the case, and it does most of its work in email, forms, and instructions.
examples: Have you already filed? If so, ignore this notice.
The lease may renew automatically. If so, you have thirty days to opt out.
Are you driving? If so, I'll ride with you.
She may have left already; if so, we'll catch her tomorrow.
Check whether the charge posted twice, and dispute it if so.
Did the tracking number ever update? If so, forward me the email.

entries.type: subordinating (elliptical clause used as a scalar tag)
entries.clause: a reduced conditional clause — "if it is even that much"
entries.pattern: [quantity or measure], if that. · [main clause] [quantity], if that. · [measure], if that, [continuation].
entries.punctuation: A comma before it and nothing after it, because it closes the clause. It joins nothing and cannot stand between two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: Tacked onto a number or a measure to say the figure is a ceiling and the truth may well be less. It is the mirror image of scalar if not, which pushes the estimate up: hundreds, if not thousands means possibly more, while a hundred, if that means probably fewer.
examples: The whole meeting took ten minutes, if that.
There were forty people in the room, if that.
He's twenty-five, if that.
We got two inches of snow, if that.
The repair will run you fifty dollars, if that.
She's been here a month, if that, and she already runs the place.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (a pro-form standing in for a two-branch alternative)
entries.register: neutral to formal; writing more than speech
entries.clause: no clause of its own — it points back at two possibilities already named
entries.pattern: [sentence]. In either case, [sentence]. · [sentence]; in either case, [sentence]. · [clause], and in either case [clause]. · [main clause] in either case (final, no comma).
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it, comma after it when it opens a clause — a comma alone in front of it is a comma splice, exactly as with otherwise and in that case. A coordinating conjunction may carry the join instead, and then the comma goes before the coordinator. Riding at the end of its own clause it takes no punctuation at all: The answer is the same in either case.
entries.meaning: Says the consequence is the same on both branches of an alternative that has just been spelled out. It is the written counterpart of either way — the same job, but at home in reports and letters where either way would sound too casual, and unlike either way it wants the two branches actually stated first.
examples: The committee may approve the plan or send it back; in either case, we hear by Friday.
She can appeal or she can refile. In either case, the clock starts over.
The tenant may cure the default or vacate; in either case, the landlord's costs are recoverable.
The result is the same in either case.
Rain would postpone the game and lightning would shorten it — in either case, nobody gets home before ten.
In either case, somebody has to tell the client before the end of the day.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (demonstrative adverbial phrase)
entries.clause: no clause of its own — it points back at a condition somebody has just put on the table
entries.pattern: [sentence]. In that case, [sentence]. · [sentence]; in that case, [sentence]. · [clause] and, in that case, [clause]. · [subject] in that case [verb phrase] (medial, rarer).
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it, comma after it when it opens a sentence. A comma alone in front of it is a comma splice: write The store's closed; in that case, we'll order in, never The store's closed, in that case we'll order in. This is exactly where it parts company with in which case, which is a relative and does take a plain comma.
entries.meaning: Picks up a condition that has just been stated — usually by somebody else — and says what follows from it. The difference from in which case is structural rather than semantic: in which case continues the sentence that raised the possibility, while in that case starts a new one, which is why it is the natural reply in conversation.
examples: "The 6:40 is sold out." "In that case, we'll drive."
You'd rather not fly? In that case, I'll price out the train.
The permit may take another month; in that case, we push the opening to spring.
She's already eaten. In that case, we can skip the reservation.
In that case, I'd rather hear it from him directly.
If the intake numbers are wrong, the whole model is wrong, and in that case we start over.

entries.type: subordinating (sentential relative)
entries.clause: a non-restrictive relative clause commenting on the whole clause before it
entries.pattern: [clause], in which case [clause]. · [sentence]. In which case, [sentence]. (informal)
entries.punctuation: A comma before it — it heads a relative clause attached to what came before, so in careful writing it does not start a new sentence, although email and speech often let it. When it does open a sentence, put a comma after it.
entries.meaning: Chains a consequence onto a possibility already stated, with which pointing back at that whole possibility. The difference from in that case is structural: in which case continues the same sentence, in that case replies to something just said.
examples: The flight may be delayed, in which case we'll rebook you on the morning departure.
She might not have gotten the email, in which case I'll resend it.
The inspection could turn up mold, in which case the sale falls through.
He may already be on his way, in which case calling won't help.
Rain is possible, in which case the reception moves indoors.

entries.type: coordinating (fixed phrase)
entries.register: neutral; the bare threat use is informal
entries.clause: coordinate clause stating the negative alternative
entries.pattern: [imperative or statement], or else [clause]. · [imperative], or else.
entries.punctuation: Comma before or else when it joins two clauses — the same rule as plain or. The bare threat takes a period, and nothing after it.
entries.meaning: Names what happens if the first clause is not carried out — the coordinated twin of unless. Do it, or else you're fired and You're fired unless you do it state the same deal from opposite ends — and note that the coordinator takes its comma while the subordinator does not. Left bare, or else is an entire threat by itself.
examples: Leave now, or else you'll hit rush hour.
Back up the drive tonight, or else you'll be sorry tomorrow.
Pay the balance by the first, or else the account goes to collections.
"Turn the music down, or else."
We need to leave by six, or else we're eating dinner at ten.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb
entries.clause: no clause of its own — it links two independent clauses as an adverb
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; otherwise, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. Otherwise, [independent clause]. · [independent clause] — otherwise [independent clause]. · [independent clause]; [subject] would otherwise [verb phrase] (medial).
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it, comma after it. We should leave now; otherwise, we'll be late. A comma alone in front of otherwise is a comma splice — the single most common punctuation error with this word, because it feels like a conjunction and is not one.
entries.meaning: States what will happen if the preceding statement is not acted on — the conjunctive-adverb equivalent of or else and the mirror image of unless. It also works backward as an inference marker: She must have left; otherwise her coat would still be here.
examples: Take the earlier train; otherwise, you'll miss the opening.
We need a deposit by Friday. Otherwise, the room goes back into inventory.
Write it down; otherwise, you'll forget by morning.
She must have left already — otherwise her coat would still be here.
The tickets are nonrefundable; otherwise, I'd have canceled weeks ago.
The deadline is firm; we'd otherwise be glad to give you another week.

entries.type: subordinating (participial, with a Latin adverb wedged inside it)
entries.register: legal (briefs, opinions, oral argument); it appears essentially nowhere else
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition — a premise conceded for the sake of argument only
entries.pattern: Assuming arguendo that [clause], [main clause]. · Assuming, arguendo, that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], assuming arguendo that [clause]. · [verb] arguendo [that-clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. Courts print it both ways — assuming arguendo that and assuming, arguendo, that with the Latin fenced in commas — and either is safe so long as a single brief keeps to one of them. Arguendo is italicized in most American legal style, though a few court styles set it roman.
variants: assuming for the sake of argument that
entries.meaning: Concedes a point without accepting it, purely in order to show that the concession does not save the other side — the lawyer's way of saying "even if you are right about that, you still lose." Assuming that takes a premise on board provisionally and reasons from it; assuming arguendo that takes it on board while making plain that the writer denies it.
examples: Assuming arguendo that the statute applies, the plaintiff still filed too late.
Assuming, arguendo, that the search was unlawful, the evidence would have been inevitably discovered.
The court observed that, assuming arguendo that a duty existed, no breach had been shown.
Assuming arguendo that the contract is ambiguous, the extrinsic evidence favors our reading.
Counsel conceded arguendo that the notice was late and argued the absence of prejudice instead.
Assuming arguendo that the officer had reasonable suspicion, the stop still lasted far too long.

entries.type: subordinating (inverted present subjunctive of be plus a complementizer)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition — a premise granted for argument
entries.pattern: Be it that [clause], [main clause]. · So be it that [clause], [main clause]. · Be it so that [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause, which is the only position the phrase takes. No if — inverting the subjunctive be in front of its subject does that work, exactly as were and had still do in modern counterfactuals.
entries.meaning: An old subjunctive formula meaning "granting that" or "even supposing that," built by putting be in front of its subject. An American meets it in Shakespeare and his contemporaries, in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century prose, and in the recitals of old deeds; the only fragments of it still alive are the concessive be it rain or shine and the standalone shrug so be it, neither of which is this conjunction.
examples: Be it that he hath wronged thee, thy revenge is no remedy.
Be it that the debt was lawfully contracted, no action lay after the term had run.
So be it that the tenant pay the rent reserved, the lease shall continue in force.
Be it that she erred in judgment, her intent was honest, and the court so found.
Be it that the witness spoke truly, the account still wants corroboration.

entries.type: subordinating (a fossilized doublet — the old conditional and reinforced by if)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition opening a new turn in a narrative
entries.pattern: But and if [clause], [main clause]. · And if [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause, which is its only position. The King James text often sets the clause off with a colon or a semicolon instead, following seventeenth-century pointing rather than modern rules; a modern editor quoting it leaves the original punctuation alone.
entries.meaning: A King James Bible formula meaning nothing more than "but if." The and in it is not the coordinator: it is the old conditional an, itself meaning "if," so the phrase stacks three conditional words on top of one another — which is why every translation after 1611 dropped it. An American meets it in the KJV, in preaching that quotes the KJV, and nowhere else.
examples: "But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming…" (Matthew 24:48)
"But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband." (1 Corinthians 7:11)
"But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned." (1 Corinthians 7:28)
"But and if ye suffer for righteousness' sake, happy are ye." (1 Peter 3:14)
But and if the tenant fail to pay the rent reserved, the term shall cease and determine.

entries.type: subordinating (a Latin ablative absolute borrowed whole; an adverbial phrase, not a conjunction)
entries.register: formal, technical Latin (economics, philosophy, legal argument)
entries.clause: no clause — a fixed Latin phrase standing in for a whole condition
entries.pattern: Ceteris paribus, [main clause]. · [main clause], ceteris paribus. · [subject], ceteris paribus, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens a sentence, comma before it when it trails, commas on both sides in the middle. American style italicizes it, though economics journals often set it roman because it has become a term of art in the field. Being an adverbial and not a connector, it cannot join two independent clauses with a comma.
entries.meaning: The Latin for all else being equal, and the standard hedge of economic reasoning: it isolates one variable by declaring every other one frozen. It survives because economics needed a compact way to say it, and outside economics, philosophy, and the occasional judicial opinion an American writer is better served by the English.
examples: Ceteris paribus, a rise in price reduces the quantity demanded.
The model predicts, ceteris paribus, that real wages track productivity.
Ceteris paribus, the defendant with counsel fares better than the one without.
Higher tariffs raise domestic prices, ceteris paribus.
Ceteris paribus, a country that saves more will invest more.
The court reasoned that, ceteris paribus, the earlier filing should control.

entries.type: subordinating (a Latin prepositional phrase used as a sentence adverbial; not a conjunction)
entries.register: formal, technical Latin (analytic philosophy, logic, appellate opinions)
entries.clause: no clause — a fixed Latin phrase pointing back at a hypothesis already granted
entries.pattern: Ex hypothesi, [main clause]. · [subject] is, ex hypothesi, [complement]. · [main clause] ex hypothesi.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens a sentence and commas on both sides in the middle; a writer who runs it into the clause without commas (the premise is ex hypothesi true) is treating it as an ordinary adverb, which is also standard. Italicized in American style. It links nothing, so two independent clauses on either side of it still need a period or a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Means "by the hypothesis already granted" — it flags that what follows is not a fresh claim but something the assumed premise already contains. Where ceteris paribus freezes the other variables, ex hypothesi reaches back to a supposition made earlier in the argument and draws out what it entails.
examples: The being in question is, ex hypothesi, perfect, so the objection cannot arise.
Ex hypothesi, the two sets have no member in common.
If the promise was gratuitous, then ex hypothesi no consideration passed.
The second premise is ex hypothesi true, and the argument turns entirely on the first.
Ex hypothesi the defendant knew nothing of the scheme; the question is whether he should have.

entries.term: if and to the extent that
entries.type: subordinating (fixed legal doublet)
entries.register: legal (credit agreements, indentures, tax and indemnity provisions)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition combining a yes-or-no test with a scope test
entries.pattern: [main clause] if and to the extent that [clause]. · If and to the extent that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] to the extent, if any, that [clause]. · [main clause] if and to the extent [past participle].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted clause; no comma when it follows the main clause, which is the usual position. Never break the doublet with a comma — the exception is the inverted to the extent, if any, that, where the commas around if any are required.
variants: to the extent, if any, that
if, and only to the extent that
entries.meaning: A drafter's belt-and-suspenders phrase asking two questions at once: does this apply at all, and if so, how far? Modern drafting guides call it redundant, on the ground that to the extent that already answers both — nothing applies to a zero extent — but it stays standard in indentures and tax language, where drafters would rather repeat themselves than litigate the point.
examples: The Borrower shall indemnify the Lender if and to the extent that such losses arise from the Borrower's negligence.
If and to the extent that any provision of this Agreement is held unenforceable, that provision shall be severed.
Amounts withheld shall be credited if and to the extent that they are actually remitted to the taxing authority.
The guaranty applies if and to the extent that the primary obligor fails to pay when due.
If and to the extent that the Trustee has actual knowledge of a default, it shall notify the holders.
This policy responds to the extent, if any, that the underlying policy does not.

entries.type: subordinating (archaic — if plus the present subjunctive be, with an optional complementizer)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition
entries.pattern: If so be that [clause], [main clause]. · If so be [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] if so be that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. Older printings use a colon or a semicolon at the seam instead, on seventeenth-century principles rather than modern ones, and a quotation should keep whatever the source had.
entries.meaning: An old way of saying "if it should turn out that" or "provided that," with the subjunctive be marking the condition as genuinely open. It is a piled-up conditional — if plus so be plus that — of the kind Early Modern English liked and modern English trimmed away. An American meets it in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare's contemporaries, and in eighteenth-century deeds.
examples: "…if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you." (Romans 8:9)
"If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious." (1 Peter 2:3)
"If so be they will hearken, and turn every man from his evil way…" (Jeremiah 26:3)
"…if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together." (Romans 8:17)
If so be that the said lands descend to the heirs male, the entail shall stand.

entries.type: subordinating (prepositional — takes a noun phrase)
entries.register: formal, legal (wills, trusts, mortgages, older statutes)
entries.clause: no clause — a noun phrase naming the act that fails to happen
entries.pattern: In default of [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] in default of [noun phrase]. · [main clause], in default whereof [clause]. (older drafting)
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, which is where it usually appears; no comma when it follows. In default whereof takes a comma before it and none after, since like failing which it heads a relative clause.
entries.meaning: The drafting formula for "if that does not happen": it names an act that was required and provides for its not being done. In default of issue, in default of payment, and in default of appointment are set phrases in wills and mortgages, and outside that world an American would write absent or simply if there is no.
examples: In default of payment, the mortgagee may enter and sell.
The estate passes to the testator's nephews in default of issue.
In default of agreement between the parties, the matter shall be referred to arbitration.
The power passes to the survivor in default of appointment by either spouse.
In default of an answer within twenty days, judgment may be entered against you.
The tenant shall repair within thirty days, in default whereof the landlord may re-enter.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (a fronted negative adverbial; not a conjunction)
entries.register: formal, legal (limitation-of-liability, indemnity, and cap provisions)
entries.clause: no clause of its own — a sentence adverbial that forces subject–auxiliary inversion when it is fronted
entries.pattern: In no event shall [subject] [bare infinitive]. · In no event will [subject] [verb phrase]. · In no event may [subject] [bare infinitive]. · uninverted: [subject] shall in no event [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma after it. It is part of the clause it inverts, not a sentence adverb like however, and a comma would cut the adverbial off from its own verb: write In no event shall the Company be liable, never In no event, shall the Company be liable. Because it joins nothing, two independent clauses on either side of it still need a period or a semicolon.
entries.meaning: The drafter's absolute negative — the flat denial that opens a limitation-of-liability clause, and the mirror image of in the event that, which opens one condition where this closes all of them. The inversion is obligatory once the phrase is fronted, by the same negative-fronting rule that gives never have I seen and not once did she complain.
examples: In no event shall the Company be liable for indirect, incidental, or consequential damages.
In no event will aggregate liability exceed the fees paid in the preceding twelve months.
In no event shall the term of this Lease extend beyond December 31, 2045.
In no event may a claim be brought more than two years after the loss.
Interest shall in no event exceed the maximum rate permitted by law.
In no event shall silence be construed as acceptance of an offer.

entries.type: subordinating (archaic); the same word is an adverb meaning "perhaps" and a noun meaning "doubt"
entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition, or of apprehension after a verb of fearing
entries.pattern: Peradventure [clause], [main clause]. · If peradventure [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] lest peradventure [clause]. · beyond peradventure of doubt (the surviving noun idiom).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause. As the bare adverb meaning "perhaps" it opens the sentence and takes its own comma in modern printing, though seventeenth-century texts leave that comma out and a quotation should not add it.
entries.meaning: The old word for "by chance," used as a conjunction meaning "if by chance" and, after a verb of fearing, "lest." Its everyday afterlife is not conditional at all: what an American actually meets is the adverb in the King James Bible (Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city) and the frozen legal noun in beyond peradventure of doubt. The conjunction itself died out with the eighteenth century.
examples: "Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city." (Genesis 18:24)
"Peradventure the woman will not be willing to follow me." (Genesis 24:5)
If peradventure the ship be lost, the underwriters shall answer for the whole.
Set a watch upon the gate, lest peradventure he come upon thee unawares.
Peradventure the heir die without issue, the land shall revert to the donor.

entries.type: subordinating; also a complementizer in noun clauses
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition; also a noun clause
entries.pattern: Whether or no [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whether or no [clause]. · [verb of knowing or asking] whether or no [clause]. · [main clause] whether [clause] or no (the split form).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it follows, and none before a noun clause — the same rules that govern whether or not.
entries.meaning: The older shape of whether or not, with the archaic sentential no where modern English puts not. It is not an error, only dated: it is thick on the ground in the King James Bible, in Milton, and in nineteenth-century novels, and an American who writes it today will be read as reaching for an antique effect.
examples: Whether or no the enterprise succeed, the attempt does him honor.
She meant to have her way, whether or no her brother approved.
I know not whether or no he will come.
Whether or no the treaty be ratified, the boundary is settled in fact.
He would have the boy schooled, whether or no the money could be found.
